strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and represents a clear conceptual shift: replacing 2D-rendered pose images with directly tokenized 3D motion (4DMoT) as the control signal, addressing a genuine limitation of prior work (pixel-level copying and loss of 3D information).

Substantial quantitative gains on the standard TikTok benchmark (FID-VID 6.98 vs. 20.64 for the second-best; best FVD, FID, and LPIPS), supported by comparisons against a broad set of recent methods including UniAnimate, MimicMotion, StableAnimator, ControlNeXt, and Human-DiT.

Thorough ablations (Table 2) covering the vector quantizer, multiple positional encoding designs (dynamic, learnable, temporal-only, spatial-only, none), and motion-aware CFG, with visual ablation (Fig. 6) that convincingly supports each design choice.

The paper is generally well-written and clearly structured; the 4D RoPE design (1D temporal + 3D spatial on joint coordinates) is intuitive and the algorithmic details in Appendix E enable reproduction.

Extensive appendix: dataset curation pipeline (shot segmentation, pose filtering, quality filtering), codebook utilization analysis, reconstruction results on unseen gymnastics data, attention map visualizations, and training curves.
Honest limitations section (non-human proportions, hand articulation, multi-person) and a discussion of misuse risks with planned safeguards; anonymous code release.
weaknesses: Fairness of the SOTA comparison is questionable: MTVCrafter fine-tunes a ~7B-parameter CogVideoX-5B base model (8 H100 GPUs), while most baselines are substantially smaller U-Net/SD-based systems. The paper does not isolate how much of the 65% FID-VID improvement comes from the 4D motion formulation versus simply using a much stronger video generation backbone; an ablation conditioning the same base model on rendered pose images would be needed to attribute the gains.

Evaluation is limited to the TikTok benchmark (sequences 335-340) and only dance motion; no additional benchmarks (e.g., fashion, cross-domain motion), no human perceptual study, and no pose-alignment metrics despite the paper's emphasis on motion accuracy.

The claimed 'raw 3D motion' is itself estimated by NLF-Pose, introducing a noisy intermediate; the paper does not quantify sensitivity to pose-estimation errors, which is important since 2D-pose methods are criticized for their conditioning source.

Some evaluation protocols are mixed: results for some baselines are re-run under the authors' setting and others are copied from original papers, which weakens comparability; details of which numbers come from where should be more explicit.
The practical scope is narrow: 512x512, 49-frame clips, ~90s inference on an H100, single-person only, and full-body dancers; the 'open-world' claim rests largely on qualitative examples.

Missing details raise reproducibility questions for the DiT training stage (e.g., whether reference-image conditioning or text branch removal affects CFG construction), and the curated 30K-clip dataset (5K motion-video pairs) release status is unclear.

Minor issues: several typos/grammar slips (e.g., 'We design 4D motion attention...We design' capitalization, 'our' lowercase, ConcrolNeXt label in Fig. 5), the Figure 7 CFG sweep only reaches 6.0 while text discusses 9.0, and Equation 2's notation (W as 'joint regressor' vs. kinematic chain) is imprecise.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated limitation of existing human image animation methods (reliance on 2D-rendered pose images) and proposes a genuinely new direction: directly tokenizing raw 3D motion (4D motion tokens) as the conditioning signal, which is a first in this task.

The technical design is coherent: a 4D motion VQVAE (4DMoT) with EMA-updated codebook, plus MV-DiT with 4D motion cross-attention and 4D RoPE (temporal + spatial). The ablations are meaningful — removing quantization, removing positional encodings, or using partial PE variants all degrade performance substantially (e.g., FVD 235.57 vs. 140.60 without PE).

Quantitative results on TikTok show a large improvement (FID-VID 6.98 vs. 20.64 for the next best), and the authors re-evaluated competing methods under a consistent protocol, which strengthens fairness of the comparison.

The paper is transparent about limitations (non-human anatomies, hand articulation, single-person constraint) and discusses potential misuse, ethics, and planned safeguards. Code and video demos are provided via an anonymous link, and appendix details (dataset curation, codebook analysis, 4D RoPE algorithm, training curves) support reproducibility.

The tokenizer analysis (Appendix D: codebook utilization, pairwise code decorrelation, reconstruction on unseen gymnastics data) provides useful evidence that the discrete motion space is well-utilized and generalizes.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level: the motion tokenizer is a fairly standard VQVAE (borrowed from motion generation works like MotionGPT/MoMask), and the conditioning mechanism is a conventional cross-attention with RoPE. The main contribution is the novel combination and application, not new architectural primitives.

There is a potential confound in the SOTA comparison: MTVCrafter is built on CogVideoX-5B (~7B trainable parameters, 8 H100s) while most baselines use much smaller U-Net backbones. The dramatic 65% FID-VID improvement may partly reflect the stronger base video model rather than the 4D motion tokenization itself. A controlled experiment (e.g., same base DiT with 2D pose-image conditioning) would substantially strengthen the central claim.

Evaluation is limited to a very small test split of TikTok (sequences 335–340, following prior work); no additional benchmark (e.g., UBC-Fashion, or a held-out split of their curated 30K dataset) is evaluated quantitatively, and no user study is reported despite claims of superior perceptual quality.

The 4D RoPE spatial coordinates come from the dataset-wide mean joint positions rather than the actual joint positions of the driving motion (per Algorithm 1), which weakens the claim of motion-specific 3D spatial cues; the benefit of this design versus per-token coordinates is not analyzed.

There is a tension between the claims and the data: Figure 1 and the abstract advertise multi-character animation, but the dataset pipeline (Appendix B) explicitly excludes multi-person clips and the method cannot support multi-person animation with different poses. The paper also relies on NLF-Pose-estimated SMPL for both training and inference, so its 'robust 3D motion' guidance inherits pose-estimation errors that are not quantified.

PSNR and SSIM are below several baselines; the authors dismiss these as low-level metrics, but this is only partially addressed, and the very large gaps on FID/FID-VID versus the modest LPIPS gap warrant more scrutiny or statistical analysis.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated novelty: directly tokenizing raw 3D/4D motion (SMPL sequences) instead of 2D-rendered pose images is a new and sensible paradigm for human image animation, addressing genuine limitations (loss of 3D cues, pixel-level pose copying) identified in prior work.

Technically sound and complete pipeline: a 4D motion VQVAE tokenizer, a motion-aware DiT with 4D RoPE and cross-attention, and a thoughtful motion-aware CFG using learnable unconditional tokens — each component is well described and supported with equations, algorithmic detail, and visualizations.

Strong quantitative results on the TikTok benchmark (FID-VID 6.98 vs 20.64 second-best; best FVD, LPIPS, FID), plus convincing qualitative generalization results across styles (anime, pixel art, statues, photorealism) and full/half-body settings.

Thorough ablations (quantizer, positional encoding variants, CFG scale) that directly support the design choices, and a good appendix covering dataset curation, codebook utilization analysis, reconstruction quality on unseen gymnastics data, and attention map analysis.
Code and video demos are released (anonymous GitHub), improving reproducibility; limitations and ethical considerations (deepfake misuse, consent, watermarking plans) are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Potential confound in the SOTA comparison: the method builds on a 7B-parameter CogVideoX-5B DiT trained with 8 H100 GPUs, whereas most baselines are U-Net models built on Stable Diffusion (~1B scale). The dramatic FID-VID improvement (65%) may partly reflect model scale and data quality rather than the 4D motion tokenization itself; a scale-matched control or same-base-model comparison is missing.

Evaluation protocol consistency concerns: some baselines are re-evaluated by the authors while others (Animate Anyone 2, Human-DiT) are quoted from original papers; such mixed reporting on the small TikTok test split (only sequences 335-340) weakens the reliability of the reported gaps.

Dependency on noisy 3D pose estimation: the whole pipeline conditions on SMPL parameters estimated by NLF-Pose, so downstream quality is bounded by estimator errors; the paper does not quantify sensitivity to pose-estimation noise or compare against alternative 3D estimators.

Inconsistency between claimed multi-character capability and training setup: Appendix B states that multi-person clips with different poses are excluded and only single-person sub-clips are used, yet Figure 1 and Figure 14 present 'multiple characters' results — these appear to involve characters sharing the same pose sequence, so the multi-character generalization claim should be scoped more carefully.

The curated dance dataset (5K SMPL motion-video pairs from web-crawled and AI-generated sources) is relatively small and its release/licensing is not clarified; generalization claims to 'open-world' motions could benefit from more diverse training data or additional benchmarks.
No user study or perceptual evaluation to complement FID/FVD metrics; SSIM/PSNR comparisons are acknowledged as weak, and some baselines lack FID-VID/FID entries, making the comparison table uneven.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing 2D-rendered pose images with directly tokenized 4D SMPL joint coordinates is a meaningful conceptual shift for pose-guided character animation, and the paper articulates the motivation (loss of depth information, pixel-level copying bias) convincingly.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art performance across all metrics on both TikTok and Fashion benchmarks, with the 18B version showing consistent gains over the 6B version, supporting the scalability claim.

Comprehensive ablation studies covering both the motion tokenizer (quantization, differential motion, 3D vs 4D quantization) and motion attention positional encodings (six PE variants), with consistent conclusions on two datasets; additional ablations (CFG scale, codebook analysis, alternative projections for the 18B model) in the appendix.

Engineering completeness: the method is instantiated on two backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B), dataset curation is described in detail (Appendix B), and 4D RoPE implementation is fully specified (Algorithm 1), which aids reproducibility.
Impressive qualitative zero-shot generalization (non-human characters, diverse styles), which, if it holds up under scrutiny, opens a genuinely new direction for pose-guided video generation.
Includes a limitations section, ethics statement, and responsible-use discussion (misuse, consent, watermarking plans).
weaknesses: Evaluation consistency concerns: the paper reports some baseline metrics copied directly from original papers and re-evaluates others (e.g., FID-VID) under its own settings. Mixing metrics obtained under different evaluation protocols weakens the comparability of Table 1/3 and inflates the apparent SOTA margin.

The central claim that 4D motion tokenization is superior to 2D-rendered pose guidance is not directly validated quantitatively: there is no experiment training the same DiT backbone with rendered SMPL/mesh/depth images versus 4D motion tokens. Appendix E.2's tokenization-vs-rendering comparison is qualitative only, so the core architectural contribution's advantage over the strongest conditioning alternative is asserted rather than measured.

Unfair backbone comparison: MTVCraft-18B is built on Wan-2.1-14B while most compared baselines are SD-1.5/SD-based models. Much of the gain may come from the stronger base video model rather than the proposed conditioning mechanism; MTVCraft-6B's narrower margins (e.g., PSNR ties with UniAnimate-DiT) partially suggest this.

Non-human and open-world generalization is showcased only with qualitative figures; no quantitative protocol (e.g., pose consistency metrics on a non-human test set, or user study) is provided to substantiate the 'unparalleled zero-shot generalization' and 'emergent ability' claims.
No human evaluation or perceptual study, which is standard for this task area given that FID/FVD/PSNR/SSIM are known to correlate poorly with animation quality and identity preservation.

Some unsupported or overclaimed statements: 'first framework that directly models raw 4D motion' is hard to verify; the claim that using dataset-averaged joint positions for 4D RoPE is 'unique' and beneficial is only supported indirectly by the PE ablation table; text says 'about 30% of codes are underutilized... improving robustness' which reads as post-hoc justification of codebook redundancy.

Known limitations are acknowledged (no multi-person support, poor hand articulation, dependence on base model), but multi-person animation and hand/finger control are increasingly expected in this sub-area; SMPL-24-joint representation fundamentally lacks hands, limiting applicability.

Data provenance: 200K web-crawled video clips with unclear licensing and consent; the ethics discussion is brief and the actual safeguards (consent verification, watermarking) are only 'planned', despite the model being commercially deployed.

strengths: The core idea is clearly motivated: replacing 2D-rendered pose images with directly tokenized 4D SMPL joint coordinates is a reasonable and novel design choice for pose-guided character animation, and the paper articulates the motivation (pixel-level copying, loss of depth information) well.

Comprehensive method description: the 4DMoT tokenizer (VQVAE over differential joint coordinates), 4D motion attention, 4D RoPE, and motion-aware CFG are all specified in enough detail (architecture, codebook size, hyperparameters, training schedule) to be reproducible in principle.

The ablation studies (Tables 2 and 4) are thorough, covering quantization, differential motion, and a wide range of positional encoding alternatives, and the appendix contains additional analyses (codebook utilization, reconstruction on unseen gymnastics data, attention map visualizations, training curves).
Scaling across two backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B) is a useful practical demonstration, and results improve consistently from 6B to 18B on both benchmarks.
Appendix is extensive, with dataset curation details, limitations, and an ethics statement provided.
weaknesses: The SOTA comparison is not scale-fair. MTVCraft-18B is built on a 14B-parameter pretrained video foundation model and finetunes ~4B new parameters, while most baselines (MimicMotion, AnimateAnyone variants, UniAnimate-DiT, etc.) are far smaller. The substantial FVD/FID gains may largely reflect backbone scale and pretraining data rather than the proposed 4D motion tokenization; a controlled comparison at matched scale/backbone is missing. The 6B variant's improvements over UniAnimate-DiT are also modest (e.g., PSNR/SSIM are comparable or worse on Fashion).

The centerpiece dataset (200K web-crawled clips, 30K curated SMPL-video pairs) is neither released nor fully documented in terms of licensing, and the web-crawled provenance raises legal/ethical questions that the ethics statement does not adequately address. Combined with the reliance on the private dataset, reproducibility of the headline results is weak.

No human evaluation or user study is provided. All quantitative evidence relies on frame-level (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FID) and distributional metrics (FVD/FID-VID), which are known to correlate poorly with perceived motion quality and identity consistency for generative video models; claims like 'state-of-the-art performance across all metrics' and 'perfectly preserves identity' are stronger than the evidence.

The zero-shot generalization to non-human subjects (animals, objects, anime/animated characters) is presented as an emergent capability of the method, but it plausibly derives from the generalization of the base video diffusion models; no controlled analysis isolates the contribution of 4D motion tokens to this behavior. Additionally, the paper freely displays copyrighted characters (Dragon Ball, Spider-Man, SpongeBob, Stitch, etc.), which is a notable IP/ethics concern.

Several design decisions are under-justified: the (x, y, z) coordinates for motion-token RoPE use dataset-averaged joint positions over all frames (a fixed, pose-independent skeleton), which seemingly discards per-frame motion information from the positional encoding; the benefit of assigning z=0 to vision tokens vs. alternatives is not analyzed; and zero-padding for cross-backbone token alignment is explained only post hoc (linear/MLP projections failed to converge), suggesting fragile design.

Some claims of novelty are overstated: tokenizing SMPL/joint data with VQVAEs is well established in motion generation, and the main novelty is the conditioning integration into video DiTs; 'the first framework that directly models raw 4D motion' is asserted without rigorous differentiation from concurrent or prior 3D-pose-conditioned approaches (e.g., DreamDance, Champ-style 3D guidance).

Presentation issues reduce polish: project page and commercial deployment URLs are left blank in the abstract; minor typos (e.g., 'Fahsion', 'preserver', inconsistent naming Wan-2-1 vs Wan-2.1); Figure 7's failure case discussion is thin.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing 2D-rendered pose images with directly tokenized 4D (3D joint coordinates over time) motion tokens for character animation. The paper convincingly argues the two limitations of 2D pose images (loss of 4D information; pixel-level copying bias) and addresses both with a coherent design.

The technical components are well-integrated: a 4D motion VQVAE (4DMoT) with differential joint coordinates, a motion-aware DiT (MV-DiT) with 4D motion attention and 4D RoPE, and motion-aware classifier-free guidance. The choice to tokenize joint coordinates rather than SMPL parameters is well justified and ablated.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art performance on both TikTok and Fashion benchmarks across all metrics (e.g., FVD 276.65 vs 402.14 for the best prior DiT method), demonstrated on two different backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan-2.1-14B), showing scalability and backbone-agnostic applicability.

Comprehensive ablations on both benchmarks covering quantization, differential motion, 3D vs 4D quantization, and multiple positional encoding designs, with clear quantitative evidence supporting each design choice. Additional analyses of codebook utilization, 4D RoPE attention maps, and motion-aware CFG further strengthen the empirical grounding.

Impressive zero-shot generalization to non-human subjects and diverse styles (Figure 1, 5, 14, 16-18), which qualitatively demonstrates genuine disentanglement of motion from appearance—a meaningful advance over pose-image-conditioned baselines that fail in these settings.

Good reproducibility posture: detailed implementation, training, and evaluation settings in the appendix, plus released code and supplementary videos; the dataset curation pipeline is described in reasonable detail.
weaknesses: The headline zero-shot generalization to non-human subjects is supported only by qualitative examples. There is no quantitative protocol (e.g., pose alignment metrics on non-human categories, or user studies) to substantiate claims of 'emergent' and 'unparalleled' generalization; the terminology is somewhat overclaimed relative to the evidence.

Evaluation methodology has minor inconsistencies: some baseline metrics are taken from original papers while FID-VID is re-evaluated by the authors; PSNR for MTVCraft-6B ties exactly with UniAnimate-DiT (19.35), yet the paper claims state-of-the-art 'across all metrics' for the 6B model. A uniform re-evaluation protocol would be more rigorous.

The training dataset of 200K web-crawled video clips raises data licensing/provenance concerns that are not fully addressed; the ethics statement is fairly generic, and the demonstration figures use numerous copyrighted characters (Dragon Ball, Spider-Man, SpongeBob, Disney characters), which may complicate the broader societal discussion.

Some scope limitations are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed: no support for multi-person animation, hand articulation failures (Figure 7), and reliance on a single estimated pose source (NLF-Pose) whose errors could propagate into the tokens—robustness to pose-estimation noise is not systematically quantified.

The 18B variant trains only newly added attention modules and uses zero-padding for dimension alignment; while ablations exist for smaller design choices, the generalization of the full recipe to other DiT backbones remains asserted rather than exhaustively validated.

No comparison against recent methods that also inject 3D/SMPL-derived guidance (e.g., Champ, DreamDance) in the quantitative tables, so the precise advantage of tokenized 4D coordinates over 3D mesh renderings is mostly supported by ablation and qualitative reasoning rather than direct benchmark comparison.
